content:
Consider two inductive types (call them Nat and Pat) that are identical up to the choice of name. I.e exact same constructors, but with every instance of the word Nat replaced with Pat. These types clearly hold the exact same information, but Lean’s kernel doesn’t recognize their equality.

My question is why not? What are the instances where you want two structurally identical types to not be regarded as identical by the kernel? I would think that if this identity was recognized, it would be a helpful way to avoid the kernel repeating work: all proofs concerning Nat could be copied over to proofs concerning Pat.

I could imagine an encoding scheme similar to the deBruijn index trick being used for the kernel to automatically detect structurally equivalent types as equal.

I could also imagine the idea of sub-inductive types being useful: one type could contain a subset of the constructors of another type, up to structural equality.

Why should choice of constructor names be the defining characteristic of identifying these "isomorphic" types? What if I had Bool and Fool, where the actual functions defined on Fool swapped the behavior of true and false?

If I understand your question correctly, neither constructor names nor type name should matter at all, just the number of constructors and constructor types matter. I shouldn’t need to define a new type Fool to encode the exact same behavior. I could just create a new version of each function defined on Bool that swaps the assignments of true and false. Fundamentally, I claim all Bool/Fool is under the hood is an inductive type with two constructors, both of type Bool

I think these would be substantial additions to the size and complexity of the kernel (particularly the second part about "copying over proofs" between types considered equal).

If we're assuming the inductive declarations are exactly the same modulo names, I think an argument in favor of just reusing the one type to begin with is more compelling than one in favor of adding complexity to the kernel to recognize some kind of equality between two or more otherwise identical types, especially when we already have options like abbrev Pat := Nat.

Oren Hartstein said:

If I understand your question correctly, neither constructor names nor type name should matter at all, just the number of constructors and constructor types matter. I shouldn’t need to define a new type Fool to encode the exact same behavior. I could just create a new version of each function defined on Bool that swaps the assignments of true and false. Fundamentally, I claim all Bool/Fool is under the hood is an inductive type with two constructors, both of type Bool

Suppose I have two inductive types, Bool and Fool. Bool has two constructors, true : Bool and false : Bool. Fool also has two constructors, which are left : Fool and right : Fool. According to your proposal, since they have the same number of constructors with the same types, Bool and Fool should be identified. But which way? I could identify left with true and right with false, or I could identify left with false and true with right.

@Aaron Liu I don’t think “which way” is the correct way to view it. I’m imagining a system where Bool and Fool would get elaborated into the exact same thing. Similar to how fun x => x and fun y => y elaborate to the same expression
And the identification would still record the order that constructors are introduced

Oren Hartstein said:

Aaron Liu I don’t think “which way” is the correct way to view it. I’m imagining a system where Bool and Fool would get elaborated into the exact same thing. Similar to how fun x => x and fun y => y elaborate to the same expression

Even in such a system, I'm hoping true and false would still elaborate to the two constructors of this inductive type (since Bool was defined with true and false as names of the constructors) and left and right would still elaborate to the two constructors of this inductive type (since Fool was defined with left and right as names of the constructors). So you still end up with two total constructors with four total names, then we must have multiple names referring to the same constructor, and then the question is which names those are.

Chris Bailey said:

If we're assuming the inductive declarations are exactly the same modulo names, I think an argument in favor of just reusing the one type to begin with is more compelling than one in favor of adding complexity to the kernel to recognize some kind of equality between two or more otherwise identical types, especially when we already have options like abbrev Pat := Nat.

Could I make the argument that this would actually save a lot of type checking work by the kernel? I wonder how many types defined within Mathlib are structurally equivalent, and how many “unique” proofs actually differ only by names and don’t need to be type checked multiple times.

This is a question that can probably be answered if you have the time and interest, my guess is that there aren't any such declarations in mathlib.

Aaron's point is a pretty good one as well.
Add and Mul have identical definitions and it would be a disaster if the kernel ever thought they were equal.
That's a great point too, for some reason I didn't think about structures; for inductives with only one constructor there are going to be quite a few.
Also things like Except and Prod, so perhaps I spoke too soon.

Lean has the property that whenever A and B are types and h : A = B is provable from the standard axioms, then elements of A and B have exactly the same VM representation. This is important because the function cast h : A -> B is a no-op in the VM (at least I think so, someone should double check me on this). If you added an axiom h : Nat = Pat, then Nat and Pat better have exactly the same VM representation otherwise the function cast h : Nat -> Pat has undefined behavior and can trigger a crash or be combined with native_decide to prove false.

Nat has a special VM representation, but let's suppose it didn't. If the two inductive types are exactly the same, then this would probably work out. But sometimes you want to add extra implementation details like computed fields which change the VM representation of a type without changing its mathematical content. As soon as you do this, your axiom h : Nat = Pat causes undefined behavior.

For example, if you swap the order of Horizontal.left and Horizontal.right, then the #eval returns Horizontal.right. This seems a little arbitrary to me, and I think avoiding arbitrary casting functions is a good reason to not have Vertical = Horizontal be provable.

inductive Vertical
| up
| down
inductive Horizontal
| left
| right

axiom h : Vertical = Horizontal
#eval cast h Vertical.up -- Horizontal.left
